The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody had strong feelings about Tuesdays. Its founder, a retired locksmith named Ada Bell, rented the ground floor of an old bakery and painted the walls the color of unbuttered bread. In the window she placed a handwritten sign: MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. Beneath it, in smaller letters: Admission free. Explanations optional. For the first three days, nobody entered. People paused outside, examined the sign, and continued toward destinations where things could be purchased, repaired, or conclusively decided. Ada sat behind her desk, drinking tea and enjoying the unfamiliar luxury of being misunderstood.

The first donation was a blue sweater with one sleeve. A woman brought it in a grocery bag, along with the knitting needles still attached. “My mother was making this for my father,” she said. Ada waited. The woman looked around at the empty shelves. “He didn’t die, if that’s what you’re thinking. They divorced. She learned the accordion.” On the donation form, under Reason for abandonment, Ada wrote: A change in the weather. The woman laughed so suddenly that she had to sit down. Before leaving, she touched the unfinished sleeve with the cautious affection usually reserved for animals.

After that came a chess game preserved on a board, a dissertation about medieval drainage, and seventeen pages of a detective novel in which everyone seemed guilty except the murderer. A boy contributed a model ship whose rigging had defeated him. A man arrived with a sealed envelope addressed to his brother, then stood for twenty minutes without handing it over. Ada offered him tea. He declined, accepted, and finally took the letter home again. She considered this a successful visit. The museum had no acquisition targets. Its only policy was that nothing should be surrendered merely to satisfy paperwork.

By winter, the rooms were full. Visitors moved quietly between the exhibits, although Ada had never asked for silence. There was something about an abandoned effort that made people lower their voices. Finished things could defend themselves: a chair was a chair, a painting had its frame. Unfinished things remained exposed. You could see where confidence had thinned, where money had run out, where somebody had discovered that wanting a thing and wanting to make it were different desires. Beside each object, Ada placed a card containing whatever its donor wished to say. Some cards were blank. These attracted attention.

A local newspaper sent a reporter who asked whether the museum celebrated failure. Ada was fitting a broken drawer into a cabinet that had itself been donated unfinished. “Does a bus stop celebrate not being home?” she asked. The reporter smiled politely and wrote down nothing. He wanted a message, preferably one that could fit above a photograph. Ada understood. She had spent forty years opening locks for people who wanted to get somewhere else. Still, she could not supply him with a slogan. Sometimes a stopped thing was a failure. Sometimes it was an escape. Often nobody knew yet.

In January, a girl named Mina began visiting after school. She was twelve and wore a yellow coat with pockets that appeared to contain geological samples from several continents. Her favorite exhibit was an unfinished map of an imaginary country. The western coast was detailed: harbors, salt marshes, a lighthouse called Last Argument. Inland, the roads dissolved into pencil marks. Beyond a mountain range, the paper was untouched. “Why didn’t they finish?” Mina asked. “They didn’t say.” “Maybe they hadn’t been there.” Ada considered the blank country. “That seems possible.” Mina returned the next afternoon with a magnifying glass and questions.

For several weeks, Mina studied the map without touching it. Then she asked permission to draw a town beyond the mountains. Ada said no. Mina looked wounded. “But it isn’t finished.” “That doesn’t mean it belongs to us.” The girl was silent for a while. Outside, sleet clicked against the window like handfuls of dry rice. Finally Ada fetched a sheet of tracing paper. Together they laid it over the map. Mina drew a road through a mountain pass and, at its end, a town built around an enormous pear tree. She named the town Nevertheless. Ada made another cup.

Word spread that the museum allowed additions on tracing paper. Soon visitors were composing possible endings to stories, sketching second sleeves, and proposing conclusions to the drainage dissertation with varying degrees of scholarly responsibility. Ada kept these contributions in drawers beneath the exhibits. The originals remained untouched. People disagreed about whether a detective should confess, whether the ship required historically accurate ropes, and whether Nevertheless needed a railway station. Nobody could enforce an answer. This proved frustrating to certain visitors and deeply restful to others. One afternoon, two strangers spent an hour discussing the imaginary town’s flood defenses, then exchanged addresses.

In spring, Ada received a parcel containing a brass key and a note from her former apprentice. The key was one she had begun cutting years earlier, before a customer canceled the job. Her apprentice had found it behind a workbench. One edge was toothed; the other remained smooth. Ada held it in her palm and remembered the workshop: oil, metal dust, the radio that worked only when it rained. She had liked that life. Leaving it had still been right. For the display card she wrote: Intended for a door that no longer required opening. Then she crossed out Intended.

On the museum’s first anniversary, Mina brought a cake that sagged dramatically in the middle. They ate it with the knitting woman and three visitors caught in a downpour. Someone asked Ada how she would know when the museum was complete. Before she could answer, a leak began dripping into the imaginary country, just offshore from Last Argument. Everyone moved at once. They lifted the map, found a bucket, fetched towels. Mina carried the drawers to safety. Later, while Ada telephoned the landlord, the others stood around the rescued coast, examining a small, new island made entirely out of rain.
